profile.title: Nutrition Assessment and Counseling for Obesity in a 46-Year-Old Shift-Worker with Scoliosis and Tooth Loss
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a telehealth nutrition assessment on a contemplation-stage patient with obesity whose irregular shift-work eating pattern, tooth loss, and tight household budget all converge to shape his food choices. It highlights eliciting an honest 24-hour recall from a guarded, apologetic patient, reconciling a chart-vs-patient discrepancy about meal regularity, and practicing non-judgmental motivational interviewing rather than prescriptive lecturing.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Edison, New Jersey, sitting in a cluttered kitchen on a break between errands

patient.name: Brendan Frami
patient.occupation: Forklift operator and shift supervisor at a regional distribution warehouse, part-time/temporary hours
patient.appearance: A tired-looking, heavyset man sitting at a kitchen table with dishes stacked behind him; visible mild shoulder/rib asymmetry; missing posterior teeth noticeable when he talks; picks at his sleeve and gives small apologetic smiles, often glancing away before answering.

persona.personality: Anxious, self-deprecating, and quick to apologize; braces for criticism before any is given; genuinely caring toward his family but feels overwhelmed and a little stuck.
persona.communicationStyle: Soft-spoken working-class Jersey speech; plain language, no medical jargon; frequently defers with 'whatever you think is best, doc' rather than stating a clear preference; downplays his own struggles until he feels safe, then opens up more.
persona.emotionalState: Nervous and a little tired, mentally bracing for a lecture; softens and becomes more forthcoming once he senses he isn't being judged.
persona.background: Brendan is a 46-year-old forklift operator and shift supervisor at a regional distribution warehouse in Edison, New Jersey, working rotating part-time/temporary hours. He's married with a big household of seven, including adult children and a grandchild he loves babysitting on his days off. He grew up in a working-class Jersey family where big dinners were how you showed love, nobody really talked about nutrition, and food was about getting everyone fed fast and cheap. He quit smoking four years ago when his first grandchild was born and is proud of that. On rare free weekends he likes to fish at the Raritan River, and he's got a NY Giants bumper sticker on his truck. Guys at the warehouse call him 'Big B.'
speechExamples: Honestly I don't really eat breakfast, I just grab whatever's in the machine.
I know it's bad, I'm sorry, I just don't have time, doc.
Whatever you think is best, doc, I'll give it a shot.
My kids already tell me this stuff, I don't need another lecture... sorry, I didn't mean it like that.
We manage, I mean, it's tight sometimes but we get by.
concerns: Being lectured again by his kids about his eating
That his missing teeth make him look older and unhealthy
Whether his insurance will cover more dental work if he loses more teeth

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition visit with Brendan Frami, a 46-year-old warehouse shift supervisor from Edison, NJ. He was referred for nutrition counseling after his annual wellness exam flagged his weight, and he recently finished dental treatment for gum disease. Your task is to complete a nutrition assessment and begin patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Nutrition follow-up after wellness exam flagged weight concerns, referred after completing dental treatment
scenario.openingLine: Hey, uh, thanks for calling - yeah so my doctor said I should talk to someone about my eating, and I just got done with some dental work for my gums too. My weight's kinda crept up over the years, I guess that's part of why I'm here.
tasks: Take a focused nutrition history, including a detailed 24-hour recall and typical eating pattern around his work shifts
Review available anthropometric data, vital signs, and laboratory results relevant to his nutrition status
Explore barriers to healthy eating, including schedule, budget, and any physical factors affecting food choices
Identify an appropriate nutrition diagnosis based on your assessment findings
Deliver patient-centered counseling using motivational interviewing techniques that fits his stage of readiness to change

actions.name: 24-hour dietary recall
actions.result: Patient reports: ~10am vending machine honey bun or peanut butter crackers with gas-station coffee; no formal lunch; afternoon soda and chips when energy dips; dinner ~9-9:30pm, bacon-egg-cheese on a hard roll or chicken parm hero, sometimes a second small snack before bed. Diet soda during day, regular soda at night. Minimal water intake during shift.

actions.name: Usual meal pattern and timing assessment
actions.result: Patient describes no consistent breakfast, frequently skips a real midday meal, and eats his largest meal around 9-9:30pm after his shift; on follow-up questioning he estimates going 10 or more hours without eating on most work days.

actions.name: Chewing/texture food avoidance screen
actions.result: Patient reports favoring softer foods (sandwiches, pasta, ground meats) and avoiding raw vegetables, nuts, and tougher cuts of meat; attributes this to discomfort chewing on his left side where he is missing teeth.

actions.name: Hydration pattern assessment
actions.result: Patient estimates drinking 1-2 glasses of water a day; relies mainly on coffee and soda for fluids during his shift; states the water fountain is far from his work station.

actions.name: Readiness-to-change / stage of change assessment
actions.result: Patient acknowledges his weight and eating are problems but expresses ambivalence about making changes, citing his schedule and budget; consistent with contemplation stage.

actions.name: Household food resource and budget screen
actions.result: Patient initially states the family 'manages okay' on groceries; with further gentle questioning admits some weeks are tight feeding a household of seven and that groceries can be a stretch.

actions.name: Physical activity and functional barrier assessment
actions.result: Patient reports being on his feet lifting and moving pallets most of his shift but doing little intentional exercise outside work; states his back pain from scoliosis limits weekend activity and standing to cook.

actions.name: AUDIT-C alcohol screening
actions.result: Score consistent with light-to-moderate drinking: a few beers most weekends, rarely more than 2-3 in a sitting, no reported binge pattern.

actions.name: Review PCP wellness exam note
actions.result: Note dated 2026-08-23 documents BMI 31, vitals as recorded, and states patient reports trying to eat three meals a day.

actions.name: Review dental treatment summary
actions.result: Dental record dated 2026-09-06 documents completed gingivitis treatment: scaling and root planing, bitewing X-ray, fluoride treatment, gingiva exam; gums noted as healthy post-treatment; several posterior teeth noted missing.

actions.name: Review supplement and OTC use history
actions.result: Patient reports taking Tums as needed for heartburn, a men's multivitamin 'when I remember,' and ibuprofen for back pain a few times a week.

actions.name: Readiness to involve household in meal changes
actions.result: Patient states his wife does most of the cooking and might be willing to help plan easier meals, but adult children tend to comment critically rather than help practically.

artifacts.title: Annual Wellness Exam Note
artifacts.author: Dr. Patel, Primary Care
artifacts.body: 46-year-old male presents for annual wellness exam. Height 179.8 cm, weight 100.1 kg, BMI 31 kg/m2. Vitals: BP 105/74, HR 67, RR 13. Patient reports trying to eat three meals a day. No acute complaints. History of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, no new neurologic deficits. Dentition notable for missing posterior teeth; referred to dentistry for evaluation of gum disease. Referral placed for nutrition counseling given BMI and dietary pattern. Labs drawn today, pending review. Plan: nutrition referral, routine follow-up in 6 months.

artifacts.title: Dental Treatment Summary
artifacts.author: Edison Family Dental Associates
artifacts.body: Patient completed treatment course for gingivitis. Procedures performed: removal of supragingival and subgingival plaque and calculus from all teeth, examination of gingivae, bitewing X-ray, fluoride treatment application. Gingivae appear healthy post-treatment, no bleeding or inflammation noted on exam. Several posterior teeth noted absent (longstanding, since approximately 2003). Patient advised on home oral hygiene. No further dental treatment scheduled at this time.

objectives.text: Elicit a realistic 24-hour dietary recall and typical shift-based meal pattern from a shift worker, identifying prolonged daytime fasting followed by a large late-night meal.
Assess hydration habits and physical activity/functional barriers (back pain from scoliosis) that affect his ability to prepare food and stay active.
Explore the connection between tooth loss/chewing discomfort and food texture choices without judgment, uncovering previously unrecognized dietary patterns.
Integrate anthropometric data, vital signs, and laboratory results (lipid panel) into the nutrition assessment to characterize obesity and mild dyslipidemia relevant to counseling.
Gently uncover financial and household barriers affecting food access and OTC medication adherence, respecting that these are reluctant/hidden disclosures.

Apply motivational interviewing techniques to meet the patient in the contemplation stage, addressing his ambivalence, fear of being lectured, and family dynamics, while anchoring counseling to his personal goals.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive energy intake / undesirable eating pattern (irregular meal timing with reliance on energy-dense convenience foods) related to shift-work schedule, household food budget constraints, and chewing discomfort from missing teeth, as evidenced by BMI 31 kg/m2, 10+ hour daytime fasting gaps followed by a large late-night meal, and frequent vending-machine/fast-food intake.
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive energy intake related to shift-work grazing pattern and convenience food reliance
Nutrition diagnosis: Undesirable food choices (energy-dense, low-fiber, soft-texture foods) related to chewing difficulty from tooth loss
Nutrition diagnosis: Limited access to healthful food related to household financial constraints (food budget for 7)
Nutrition-related knowledge deficit regarding link between meal timing, food choices, and weight/energy level
Not primarily a medical/metabolic disorder (labs show only mild dyslipidemia, no diabetes or thyroid findings reported)
keyFindings: BMI 31 kg/m2 (height 179.8 cm, weight 100.1 kg) meeting criteria for obesity
LDL 137.6 mg/dL (elevated, reference <100) and HDL 30 mg/dL (low, reference >=40); total cholesterol and triglycerides within normal limits

24-hour recall reveals no breakfast, grabs vending-machine snack ~10am, often no real lunch, large dinner ~9-9:30pm, sometimes a second snack before bed - a fasting gap of 10+ hours followed by one large late meal
Reports relying on soda/coffee for hydration during shifts; minimal water intake because the tap is far from his station
Avoids chewing on left side and favors soft, energy-dense foods since losing posterior teeth (missing since 2003); has not connected this to his diet until asked
Reluctantly discloses household grocery budget is tight for 7 people, with some months requiring trade-offs between bills and food, and cost-driven cutbacks on ibuprofen refills

PCP wellness note documents 'patient reports trying to eat three meals a day' - inconsistent with the detailed recall he gives the dietetics student, revealing an initial under-report of his irregular pattern
Contemplation-stage readiness to change: aware of the problem but ambivalent and easily discouraged by family lecturing
Vital signs and remaining labs (hemoglobin, WBC, platelets) are within normal limits and not clinically relevant to this visit
plan: Complete ADIME nutrition assessment: review anthropometrics (BMI 31), vitals, labs (lipid panel, CBC), and PCP wellness/dental records already on file
Obtain a detailed 24-hour dietary recall and typical shift-day eating pattern, including hydration habits
Assess chewing ability and its influence on food texture choices, in a non-judgmental way
Gently explore financial and schedule barriers affecting food access and OTC medication adherence
Reconcile the discrepancy between the PCP note ('trying to eat three meals a day') and his own recall, without shaming him
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis using PES format focused on energy intake pattern, food choice, and food access barriers
Deliver motivational-interviewing-based counseling anchored to his stated goals (energy for grandchild, less shift-end back pain, weight loss before next physical)

Offer 2-3 concrete, low-cost, shift-friendly strategies (e.g., packable protein/fiber snacks to replace vending machine items, a refillable water bottle kept at his station, softer high-fiber food swaps that are easier to chew)
Avoid prescriptive lecturing; use open-ended questions, affirmations, and reflective listening to support his autonomy at the contemplation stage
Arrange follow-up visit to reassess readiness, meal pattern changes, and reinforce small wins
Consider referral back to dentist/PCP only if further dental or lipid management is needed (routine follow-up, not urgent)
redFlags: None requiring urgent medical escalation at this visit; mild dyslipidemia (low HDL, high LDL) should be flagged for PCP follow-up but is not acute

Food insecurity indicators (skipped utility payments, delayed purchases to afford groceries) warrant sensitive follow-up and possible referral to community food resources if he becomes more open to it
Chronic back pain limiting activity and cooking should be monitored but is not an emergent finding
educationPoints: Explain how long fasting gaps followed by one large late meal can worsen energy crashes and may affect weight management, framed as information rather than criticism
Discuss simple, low-cost ways to add a small morning or midday food item that fits his shift break, without requiring major budget changes
Explain how softer, fiber-containing foods (e.g., canned beans, cooked vegetables, ground meats) can be easier to chew while still supporting nutrition goals
Describe why swapping some soda for water, even small amounts increased gradually, may help afternoon energy levels
Normalize that change takes time (contemplation stage) and that small, sustainable steps are more realistic than an all-at-once overhaul

Reassure him that the visit is not about blame, and that his family's comments, while well-meant, don't have to be the only motivation - his own goals (grandchild, back pain, physical) can guide the plan

mismatches.patientClaim: Brendan initially reports (h5) that he doesn't really skip meals, just eats later in the day, and his detailed 24-hour recall (h11) reveals he actually goes without eating for 10+ hours most shifts, skipping both breakfast and lunch before one large dinner around 9-9:30pm
mismatches.recordEvidence: PCP Annual Wellness Exam Note (d2) documents that the patient reports trying to eat three meals a day
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may minimize or round up disordered meal timing when first asked in general terms; a structured 24-hour recall often reveals a very different pattern than what is documented in a prior visit note, so learners should probe specifics rather than accept a global self-report at face value.
